Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-16
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Jordan Liu (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Aurora Product), Ethan Brooks (Aurora Eng), Lina Gomez (Aurora Platform)

Summary:
Quick sandbox/demo of Redwood hosted chat + console Optimize hints. Focus on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and retry/backoff patterns for production chat. Customer asked about latency/cost tradeoffs, VPC/private options, and audit/logging.

Topics:
- Console quick tour: live sandbox, token breakdown, latency per-token
- Streaming vs sync and partial outputs + client side handling
- Retry/backoff patterns and idempotency tokens
- Batching and caching recommendations from Optimize
- Security questions: SOC2, KMS, VPC mention

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex at Redwood, and with me is Jordan our solutions engineer. How are you doing today?
[00:07] Maya Patel: Good, thanks. We just want a short hands-on.. yeah.. to see how streaming behaves for our chat use cases.
[00:12] Ethan Brooks: And also, quick sanity check on retries. We've had some odd partial streams with other vendors.
[00:17] Jordan Liu: Totally. We'll start in the sandbox, do a quick live gen, then show the console Optimize suggestions for batching/caching and finally the retry patterns we recommend. Quick question — are you looking to do hosted or private initially?
[00:30] Lina Gomez: Hosted to start. Might move to VPC later if compliance requires.
[00:34] Alex Carter: Great, hosted is the fastest onramp. Note we do offer Redwood Private for VPC/on-prem later if you need KMS or specific network controls.
[00:41] Ethan Brooks: Do you have SOC2 and exportable audit logs?
[00:43] Jordan Liu: Yes SOC 2 Type II — we can send the security pack. Logs are available via the console and can be exported; audit trails show model version, request id, and token counts.
[00:52] Maya Patel: Awesome. Let's go live if that's okay.
[00:55] Jordan Liu: Cool. I'm pasting a short prompt set into the sandbox now. This is a conversational assistant prompt, few-shot, and then a user message. I'm setting temperature to 0.2 to keep responses deterministic and max_tokens to 256. Note in the console you can toggle streaming on/off.
[01:12] [Jordan starts demo; keyboard/tapping noises in background]
[01:20] Jordan Liu: Alright you should see partial chunks come in — streaming is chunked by token groups; the client receives deltas progressively. If you're doing chat UI, typically you show a partial render then commit when the stream finishes or on notable punctuation.
[01:34] Ethan Brooks: We saw in a previous provider that sometimes the stream ended with an error and client never reconciled the partial result — what's your recommended approach?
[01:42] Jordan Liu: Two-part approach: 1) Use an idempotency token per user-turn so retries are deduped server-side, 2) implement a bounded backoff + reconciliation — if final token event doesn't arrive, you either fetch the sync complete endpoint or retry the generation with same idempotency key. We also surface a final 'end_of_response' signal in the event stream.
[02:03] Maya Patel: Is the idempotency token something Redwood manages or do we provide it?
[02:07] Alex Carter: You provide it per request. The SDK convenience helpers set it for you often, but it's best to pass one from your app for server-side dedupe.
[02:15] Lina Gomez: What about concurrency and token throughput caps? Our use is high concurrency during peak promotions.
[02:21] Jordan Liu: For hosted we expose rate limits and concurrency; you can request quota increases. For high-throughput you can use dedicated pools later. Also Optimize will suggest batching windows if your average prompt length and sequence lengths align — that reduces per-token cost.
[02:36] Ethan Brooks: Can you show token breakdown in the console?
[02:39] Jordan Liu: Sure. Switching to the token tab — here you'll see prompt tokens vs completion tokens, cost estimates, and a latency histogram. For this sample, prompt is 80 tokens, completion so far 120, estimate cost ~0.0012 per request. (note: example numbers)
[02:58] Maya Patel: The console shows a 'suggested quantization' flag — what's that about?
[03:02] Jordan Liu: That's from Optimize. We give model + quantization recommendations to balance cost/latency. For chat-heavy short-turn workloads we might suggest int8 or 4-bit quant profiles on compatible model variants.
[03:12] Ethan Brooks: Are there any gotchas with streaming + quantized models?
[03:16] Jordan Liu: Mostly around warmup and KV-cache effects — you might see a slightly different token cadence. But the runtime has kernel selection that smooths latency for common lengths.
[03:24] [short pause, browser click]
[03:30] Maya Patel: Okay, can you simulate a transient error and show retry behavior?
[03:33] Jordan Liu: Yep — I'll trigger a forced 500 on the next chunk. Watch the client.
[03:38] [demo noise]
[03:41] Jordan Liu: There — stream returned a 500 mid-response; console shows event with request_id ff-demo-112, and we recommend the client detect that and call the sync /complete or retry with backoff. Our suggested backoff policy in the docs is exponential with jitter: start at 200ms, double, cap ~5s, with max attempts 3 for interactive flows.
[04:02] Ethan Brooks: If we retry with same idempotency token, server will dedupe?
[04:06] Jordan Liu: Exactly. Repeat with same idempotency key will return the same completed response when available — dedupe handled server-side.
[04:12] Maya Patel: And for streaming clients, what's the best way to display partials vs final?
[04:16] Jordan Liu: Show partials, but mark them as provisional. On final event, replace or commit. If you keep interim tokens and then get a duplicate on final, use the request id or idempotency token to dedupe. Also persist the final full string server-side for user history.
[04:33] Alex Carter: Quick note on timeouts: set conservative client-side timeouts for first token (TTFT) and for overall completion. We surface TTFT from the console so you can set sensible thresholds.
[04:43] Lina Gomez: For pilot sizing, what sample size do you need for cost projection?
[04:47] Jordan Liu: ~1k representative requests with avg prompt+completion lengths and distribution of concurrent users—Optimize will run projections and suggest batching/KV-cache settings.
[04:57] Maya Patel: Can Optimize do automatic caching suggestions?
[04:59] Jordan Liu: Yes, Optimize flags prefix patterns that are cacheable (for assistant-style responses where the prompt contains largely static system messages). It will recommend prefix caching and KV-cache TTLs.
[05:12] Ethan Brooks: Any mentions of competitor lock-in with your hosted offering?
[05:15] Alex Carter: We support standard model catalog and make it easy to pin model versions; moving to Dedicated or Private keeps the API consistent, so you avoid big rewrites.
[05:24] Maya Patel: About security — if we go to VPC later, is there an air-gapped option?
[05:29] Jordan Liu: There is an on-prem package we can discuss — it’s a longer lead time, but supported for enterprise. We'll include details in the security doc we send.
[05:38] [demo continues — Jordan runs a short high-concurrency test to show token latency under parallel requests]
[06:05] Jordan Liu: You can see here under parallelism 20 the per-token latency rises slightly; that's expected. Optimize suggests windowed batching (50ms) to recover some throughput.
[06:17] Ethan Brooks: What about partial transcriptions, sometimes words are mis-ordered — is that from our client or the server?
[06:22] Jordan Liu: Could be either; transcripts can have ASR-style mishears — but for token order, the runtime emits tokens in generation order. If you see reordering, it might be client-side rendering buffering.
[06:34] Maya Patel: We have a question — can we stream embeddings or only generations?
[06:38] Alex Carter: Embeddings are usually sync endpoints; streaming is for generation. You can stream scoring/reranking in a custom flow but not typical embedding APIs.
[06:48] Lina Gomez: For the pilot, we care a lot about cost predictability. Does your console give per-route breakdowns?
[06:54] Jordan Liu: Yes per-route and per-model. You can tag endpoints, and we produce cost/run charts. You can also set quotas to avoid surprise spend.
[07:05] Maya Patel: Any gotchas with prompt injection and streaming?
[07:09] Jordan Liu: Same risks as sync; we recommend output filters and safety checks. We also offer tools to run prompts through a safety model post-generation.
[07:20] [wrap-up signals]
[07:22] Alex Carter: To wrap — we'll send the pilot plan and pricing. Jordan will send a short clip of the token breakdown and Optimize recommendations. Maya, you'll share sample prompts and SLOs. Anything else?
[07:35] Maya Patel: No that's great. One small ask — could we get a sample backoff snippet for our React client?
[07:40] Jordan Liu: Yep I'll paste a tiny pseudo-code and include it in the follow-up. We'll include a note about idempotency tokens and reconciling partials.
[07:50] Ethan Brooks: Thanks all, very helpful.
[07:52] Alex Carter: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.

Notes about transcript quality: automated transcript had a few recognition errors (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache, "Redwood Dedicate" instead of Dedicated) — cleaned lightly but retained some rawness.

End of meeting.
